In 1857, the year of the Indian Rebellion, the British government in India founded universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. They were the first modern universities in South Asia.

They followed from the choice of English education in 1835 (see Macaulay's Minute) and from an order of 1854 calling for a full system from village schools upward. The model was the University of London. The universities did not teach. They set courses, held examinations and gave degrees, and the teaching was done in colleges linked to them, from Lahore to Rangoon.

Only two students passed the first degree examination at Calcutta in 1858. One was Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, later the author of Anandamath. Numbers grew fast. Women were admitted from 1878, and Kadambini Ganguly and Chandramukhi Basu took their degrees at Calcutta in 1883, before women could do so at Oxford or Cambridge.

The system was built on English, examinations and rote learning, and it led mostly to government clerkships and the law. It also produced the scientists J. C. Bose and C. V. Raman and most leaders of the national movement. Graduates who could not find posts worthy of them became its sharpest critics.

More universities followed at Lahore in 1882 and Allahabad in 1887.
sum: In 1857, the year of the Indian Rebellion, the British government in India founded universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. They were the first modern universities in South Asia.
